purpose: Oxycodone is used to relieve moderate to severe pain that other pain medicines have not been able to control. It may be used for pain caused by injury, surgery, or conditions like cancer. It is only prescribed when your doctor feels the benefits outweigh the risks.
how_it_works: Oxycodone works by attaching to special receptors in your brain and spinal cord called opioid receptors. When it attaches to these receptors, it blocks pain signals from reaching your brain, making you feel less pain. It also changes how your brain emotionally responds to pain, which helps you feel more comfortable.
common_side_effects: Constipation (very common — drink water and eat fiber), nausea or upset stomach, drowsiness or feeling sleepy, dizziness or lightheadedness, headache, dry mouth, and sweating. These are common especially when you first start taking it.
warnings: This medication is habit-forming and can lead to physical dependence or addiction — take it exactly as prescribed and never share it with others. It can cause dangerously slow or stopped breathing, especially if you take too much or mix it with alcohol, sleeping pills, or anti-anxiety medicines. Do not stop taking it suddenly without talking to your doctor, as this can cause withdrawal symptoms. Keep it locked away and out of reach of children — accidental ingestion can be fatal for a child.
typical_dosing: Dosing is very personalized and your doctor will start you on the lowest dose that controls your pain. Immediate-release tablets are typically taken every 4 to 6 hours as needed. Extended-release tablets (like OxyContin) are taken every 12 hours and must be swallowed whole — never crush, chew, or break them. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions.
